title: Roman, step by step — where is the telescope now?
hb_cap: A radio signal now needs {s} seconds to reach Roman — the mission's growing heartbeat. At L2 it will be 5.0 seconds, one way.
hb_note: Watch the pulse — it crosses the strip in true real time, {s} s each way, a little slower every day. The reply turns straight around.

p_tel_blurb: A 2.4-meter primary mirror, the same diameter as Hubble's but less than a quarter of its weight, feeds light to both science instruments. The barrel shape blocks stray light from the Sun, Earth, and Moon, and the visor-like aperture cover on top opens in the first days of flight.
p_wfi_blurb: Roman's main camera: 18 infrared detectors stitched into 300-megapixel frames that cover about 100 times more sky than Hubble in a single shot, at matching sharpness — the engine of surveys a thousand times faster. It wakes a few weeks into the cruise.
p_cgi_blurb: Blocks a star's glare so planets next to it can be photographed directly. On Roman it is a demonstration aiming at Jupiter-like worlds — a stepping stone toward imaging Earth-like planets with future missions. It powers on within days of launch.
p_sass_blurb: One structure, two jobs: its solar panels generate the observatory's electricity while shading the telescope from the Sun. Together with the lower instrument sun shade, it keeps the cold, light-sensitive side permanently in shadow. Deployed 1 h 23 m after launch.
p_oss_blurb: The main body everything bolts onto, including the carrier that keeps both instruments aligned with the telescope. Its rear modules hold power and data handling, six spinning reaction wheels that point the observatory, nearly a ton of propellant, and a 10-terabyte recorder.
p_com_blurb: The high-gain antenna on its boom streams about 1.4 terabytes of science data home every day — the highest rate of any NASA astrophysics mission — through the Deep Space Network dishes in the next section. Smaller antennas handle commands and tracking.
d1_x: Open and generating power — confirmed on launch morning.
d2_x: Opened together with the panels; keeps the instruments in shadow. NASA's render groups it with the sun shield.
d3_x: The main data dish unfolds — after this, the 1.4 TB-per-day downlink is available.
d4_x: The visor lifts off the telescope's mouth; the render highlights the whole telescope assembly.
d5_x: Not a moving part — the instrument boots up for its first health checks.
